Stage 3 · Grammar

will and might

Two words, one difference: how sure you are.

Read these four sentences from the text you are going to read.
  • Cities will get quieter.
  • Traffic jams won’t disappear by themselves.
  • Cars might disappear from city centres.
  • Flying taxis might not replace the train.
In some of the sentences the writer is sure and in others the writer is not. Which word shows that the writer is not sure?
How sure are you?
will / won’t — I am suremight / might not — it is possible
PositiveCities will get quieter.Cars might disappear from the centre.
NegativeTraffic jams won’t disappear.Flying taxis might not replace the train.
QuestionWill fares go up?— we do not normally ask questions with might
Short answerYes, they will. / No, they won’t.Possibly. / They might.
The verb after italways the plain verb, with no to and no -s: it will work, it might work
Softer willI think fares will go up.  ·  Fares will probably go up.  ·  They probably won’t go up.
Time wordsin the future · in twenty years · by 2045 · one day · soon

MEANING. Will is a prediction you are sure about. Might is a prediction you are not sure about — roughly a fifty-fifty chance.

FORM. Both take the plain verb: it will rain, it might rain. Never will to rain, never it might rains.

The mistake to watch: might not has no short form in careful writing. Write might not, not mightn’t.

MEANING. Use will when you are sure about the future: Electric buses will be normal in ten years. Use might when it is only possible: Flying taxis might arrive one day.

FORM. will / won’t / might / might not + the plain verb. The verb never changes: he will go, not he will goes; it might rain, not it might to rain.

SOFTENING. English speakers rarely sound one hundred per cent certain. I think… will, probably will and probably won’t sit between will and might.

Two mistakes to watch: might is not used to make questions (say Will fares go up?), and might not is written in full, not as mightn’t.

This is not the only future you know. Going to and the Present Continuous, from Unit 4, are for plans and arrangements. Will and might are for predictions. In Lesson 25 will comes back inside the first conditional.

Full grammar reference — will and might for predictions

Form

PositiveCities will be quieter. · It might rain later.
NegativeTraffic jams won’t disappear. · It might not work.
QuestionWill fares go up? · (we do not normally ask questions with might)
Short answersYes, they will. / No, it won’t.
Form rulewill and might are followed by the plain verb — no to, no -s.

Spelling and sound

will not → won’t. I will → I’ll, they will → they’ll.

When and why we use it

  • will = you are fairly sure. might = it is possible, but you are not sure.
  • Will is also used for a decision made as you speak: — It’s cold. — I’ll close the window.
  • Soften a prediction with I think, probably or perhaps: I think fares will probably go up.
  • Probably goes after will but before won’t: It will probably rain. / It probably won’t rain.

Signal words

in the future · in twenty years · by 2045 · probably · perhaps · I think… · I’m sure…

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • It will to rain. → It will rain.No to after will.
  • She will goes. → She will go.No -s after will.
  • It might to happen. → It might happen.Same rule for might.
  • I think it won’t probably rain. → I think it probably won’t rain.Probably goes before the negative.

Don’t confuse it with

will = a prediction or a decision made now. going to (Unit 4) = a plan you already had, or evidence you can see.

Stage 5 · Main input

Reading

What has already changed, and what the experts are ready to promise.

Before you read: which of these do you think will be normal in your city in twenty years?

Choose two. Then read and see whether the text agrees with you.

No right answer yet. This is your prediction.

Getting around in 2045

Nobody can predict the future perfectly. But look at what has already happened, and some of it becomes easier to guess.

In the last twenty years the picture has changed fast. Shenzhen, a Chinese city of twelve million people, replaced every diesel bus with an electric one and cut its fuel use sharply. Paris has built hundreds of kilometres of new cycle lanes. Dozens of countries have opened high-speed lines, and a journey that once took a whole day now takes three hours.

So what will happen next? Experts are confident about some of it. Cities will get quieter, because electric engines make almost no noise. The air will get cleaner: there will be less pollution from petrol and diesel. Public transport will become more efficient — buses will arrive when the app says they will, and one bus pass will work on every service in the city. Fares might go up, though. Clean transport is not cheap.

Other things are far less certain. Cars might disappear from city centres completely — or they might not. Some people think we will all travel in driverless taxis; others are not so sure. Flying taxis might work for short journeys between airports, but they probably won’t replace the train.

One prediction is safe. Traffic jams won’t disappear by themselves. If a city wants greener streets, it has to build the cycle lanes and the tracks first. The technology is the easy part.

And the people who live far from any main road? In small towns the bus is often the only service, and it is not always reliable. New developments — electric minibuses you order on your phone — might finally make village transport convenient.

Sources. Written for this course from public reporting: Shenzhen’s switch to an all-electric bus fleet (2017) · City of Paris cycle-network figures · UIC high-speed rail statistics. Everything after ‘So what will happen next?’ is written as a prediction, not as a fact.
